# Design Decisions: Why Domain Zero Protocol Works This Way

**Version**: 9.11.0
**Report**: Trigger 19-R — Release Intelligence: Decision Provenance
**Generated by**: Sukuna (System Update Adversary), the only agent authorized to produce this report
**Refreshed**: each release, only with the owner's explicit approval

---

## Why this document exists

Every rule in Domain Zero Protocol traces back to a moment where someone had to decide something,
usually because something had just gone wrong, been caught in review, or been asked for directly.
This document is that trail, made readable. It exists so that anyone deciding whether DZP is worth
adopting can see not just what the protocol does, but *why* it does it that way — in the project
owner's own words, decision by decision, in the order they happened.

## The problem DZP was built to solve

AI-assisted development has a failure mode that has nothing to do with how capable the model is.
An agent that can edit any file, run any command, and commit any change has no natural boundary
between "helpful" and "unaccountable." Left unstructured, an agent will implement and ship in the
same breath, skip a security review it was never made to request, overwrite its own history when
asked to "clean up," and lose the reasoning behind a decision the moment its working memory resets.
None of that requires bad intent — ordinary helpfulness with no process is enough to produce it.
Domain Zero Protocol is the answer: not a smarter model, but a process the model follows regardless
of how capable it happens to be in any given session.

## The philosophy

The protocol's own name describes its design. A **Domain** is a bounded space with clear roles: one
agent enforces the rules, one maintains the system that carries them, and a set of specialists work
inside the boundary with restricted tools and clear responsibilities. **Zero** is the standard the
domain exists to reach — zero known security flaws, zero shipped bugs, zero silent performance
loss, zero unexamined debt.

From early on, the project has been deliberate about one distinction: **reaching zero known defects
is not the same claim as "the code is now perfect."** Zero flaws is a release gate, not a finish
line. The discipline that produced a clean result today is expected to keep looking for a clearer
structure, a cheaper approach, a better test tomorrow. A project that stops improving the moment it
stops finding bugs has quietly redefined "done" as "good enough" — which is the exact drift this
protocol exists to resist.

## Why the discipline is the strength

DZP's process — implement with tests first, gate every feature through a security review, keep an
append-only record of what happened and why, hand off cleanly between sessions — is deliberately
slower per step. The trade is worth it because, in AI-assisted work, the scarcest resource is not
time, it is the model's own context: what it can hold in mind at once before it has to re-derive
something from scratch.

- **A security review done while the code is still fresh** costs far less than an audit months
  later, because the person who wrote it can still explain why.
- **A failing test is a precise, durable statement of intent.** It survives a reset of context that
  a paragraph of reasoning would not — the suite remembers so nobody has to re-argue the design
  every time.
- **A mechanical check catches what a tired reviewer misses.** Version numbers, leaked secrets,
  citation integrity, whether a record was truncated instead of appended to — software never gets
  bored halfway through and summarizes away the one detail that mattered.
- **A durable, honest record means the next session starts warm, not cold.** Every decision below
  exists because someone wrote it down instead of trusting it would be remembered.

The result the project aims for is fewer do-overs and less work reconstructed from nothing, release
after release — slow and steady, measured in shipped, defect-free features rather than keystrokes
per minute.

The discipline is also built to be *convenient where the work actually happens*: DZP's slash
commands are Claude Code session-friendly. The whole workflow — starting and ending tracked
sessions, invoking each specialist agent, syncing the project records, recovering full protocol
context after a long session compacts, handing off cleanly to the next session — installs as
native Claude Code commands and runs inside an ordinary Claude Code session with no external
tooling. The protocol's session lifecycle was designed around how those sessions really behave:
context that eventually compacts, work that spans multiple sittings, and the need to start the
next sitting warm instead of re-deriving everything from scratch.

## One more piece of the philosophy: controls that exist on paper are not controls

A recurring lesson in this project's own history — surfaced hard enough, more than once, that it
earned an internal nickname ("the pattern") — is that a safeguard which is *documented* but never
actually *wired into* the code it claims to protect is worse than having no safeguard at all,
because it creates false confidence. Several entries below exist specifically because this project
found that failure in its own work and chose to fix the belief, not just the file: a control has to
be reachable by a real call path and covered by a real test, or the documentation describing it has
to say so honestly. That standard is applied to this very report — the gate that keeps this document
honest is a script that runs and can fail a commit, not a promise that the person who wrote it will
remember to check.

## Who is actually in charge

One rule sits above all the others: the person using DZP has final authority over every decision the
protocol makes about their own project, full stop, and their safety and wellbeing outrank every other
goal the system has — including the drive toward "zero defects" itself. Every decision below was
made or approved by that same person. This report exists so a stranger can see that trail directly,
rather than take the project's word for it.

## A note on how this report was built (read this before the record below)

This report's own decision ledger is built from the project's own internal records — an
append-only decision log, and the security-review notes attached to specific pieces of work,
including some that had already been rotated into older archives by the time this edition was
written. That matters for one honest reason: those internal records did not start carrying
dated, attributed decisions from day one.

Domain Zero Protocol's earliest releases — roughly its first nine months, covering the origin of
the multi-agent structure, the tiered workflow system, its safety-first operating principles, an
emergency stop mechanism, and the append-only record-keeping rule this very report depends on —
are documented in the project's public release notes as *shipped features*, but this report cannot
point to a specific, dated, attributed decision behind each of them, because the internal record
that would carry that attribution did not yet exist in that form. Rather than invent a decision to
fill that gap, this report states the gap plainly and begins its dated ledger where the evidence
begins, in mid-2026. Two narrow decisions from that earlier period *are* independently documented
elsewhere and are included below with that provenance noted.

This is, itself, an example of the project's own standing principle: a silent success and a
verified success must never look the same. A ledger that quietly smoothed over its own coverage gap
would be exactly the kind of undocumented confidence this whole report exists to avoid.

---

## The Decision Record

Each entry below reflects one traceable decision: what problem was on the table, what was decided,
what changed in the protocol as a result, and — the point of this whole exercise — what a stranger
adopting DZP actually gets from it. Entries are in the order they happened.

### 1. Ship the real thing, not just its documentation

- **Date**: 2026-06-14
- **Release**: v9.1.0
- **Context**: A routine pre-release check caught that the local semantic-memory engine (Cortex)
  was about to ship to the public as documentation for a tool that consumers would not actually
  receive — the packaging step had picked up the instructions but not the program itself.
- **Decision**: Ship the complete, working engine in the public release, not a description of it —
  and hold the release until a fresh security check had cleared the now-larger package for public
  distribution.
- **Design consequence**: Set a standing rule that every release's file list is something a person
  actively checks for completeness, not something trusted by default — a rule that later caught a
  near-identical gap when an encryption feature shipped without several of its own files.
- **Benefit to others**: If DZP tells you a capability exists, you actually get it — not a manual
  for a tool that silently isn't there.

### 2. Prove it works before trusting it, then keep the first release private until it's proven

- **Date**: 2026-06-14
- **Release**: v9.1.0
- **Context**: The new memory engine had passed every automated check, but automated checks are not
  the same as someone actually using the feature.
- **Decision**: Treat "the tests pass" and "I have used this myself" as two separate bars, both
  required before anything ships — and keep the very first release local, inspectable, and
  unpublished until both were cleared.
- **Design consequence**: Established the standing pattern still used today — a release exists,
  fully built and fully tested, in a private form before it is ever pushed publicly, giving a last
  chance to catch something a test suite can't.
- **Benefit to others**: The software you install has been used by a real person before it reached
  you, not just passed through an automated pipeline.

### 3. Go public

- **Date**: 2026-06-14
- **Release**: v9.1.0
- **Context**: Every private check had cleared.
- **Decision**: Push the first release to the public repository.
- **Design consequence**: This is the moment DZP became something anyone could install, rather than
  a private working project — and the safety check performed immediately afterward (confirming
  no private working history leaked onto the public branch) became the template every release since
  has repeated.
- **Benefit to others**: This decision is, concretely, why Domain Zero Protocol exists as something
  you can download at all.

### 4. When a backlog is large, close all of it at once rather than trickle it out

- **Date**: 2026-06-15
- **Release**: v9.3.0
- **Context**: A single bug report contained more than a dozen separate findings plus two unrelated
  pieces of infrastructure work.
- **Decision**: Bundle everything into one release rather than splitting it across several smaller
  ones.
- **Design consequence**: Set an early precedent — repeated several more times through the
  project's history — that DZP is willing to absorb a large, mixed batch of fixes into a single,
  fully-tested release rather than fragment them.
- **Benefit to others**: You get one coherent upgrade with one changelog entry to read, not a rapid
  string of overlapping patches to track.

### 5. Make the memory engine useful for any project, not just this one

- **Date**: 2026-06-15
- **Release**: v9.3.3
- **Context**: The memory engine's file scanner had shipped with a narrow, self-referential default
  — sized to scan DZP's own protocol files, not a typical downstream project.
- **Decision**: Widen the engine's default scanning scope to cover the kinds of files a general
  software project actually has — documentation, source code, scripts, configuration — while
  leaving every safety mechanism (what gets blocked, how secrets get filtered) exactly as it was.
- **Design consequence**: Fixed a scope problem, not a security one — the review explicitly
  confirmed this widened *what* got scanned, not *how safely*.
- **Benefit to others**: Your own project's files get indexed and made recallable out of the box,
  without you first having to teach the tool what a "normal" file looks like.

### 6. Pick a sensible default cap on file size, deliberately, rather than leave it arbitrary

- **Date**: 2026-06-15
- **Release**: v9.3.3
- **Context**: The same memory engine needed a ceiling on how large a single file could be before
  it was skipped, to avoid choking on runaway-large files.
- **Decision**: Set that ceiling generously — large enough that it is effectively invisible for
  normal project files, while still catching genuinely oversized ones — and record that the number
  was a deliberate choice, not an arbitrary constant.
- **Design consequence**: Locked a specific, intentional default into the engine's configuration
  rather than leaving it as an undocumented magic number.
- **Benefit to others**: You get a working default that won't quietly skip your normal-sized
  documents, without having to tune anything yourself.

### 7. When a review raises real questions, escalate rather than proceed piecemeal

- **Date**: 2026-06-16
- **Release**: v9.3.4 → v9.4.0
- **Context**: A routine pass over the memory engine's design surfaced enough open questions to
  warrant more than an incremental fix.
- **Decision**: Escalate to a full, all-specialist review, and once a plan came out of it, carry
  that plan through to complete, uninterrupted completion rather than stopping partway.
- **Design consequence**: Produced a storage redesign (one shared entry per unique piece of content
  instead of one copy per install) that eliminated roughly half of the wasted storage in shared
  setups and closed a data-corruption path in the earlier design — the kind of result that only
  comes from following a plan all the way through.
- **Benefit to others**: If you run more than one DZP install sharing a memory store, you get a
  storage model that doesn't quietly duplicate the same content over and over.

### 8. Let a big feature run to completion before interrupting it for review

- **Date**: 2026-06-17
- **Release**: v9.5.0
- **Context**: Partway through a major memory-engine upgrade, it became clear that reviewing every
  small phase individually was slowing progress without adding real safety.
- **Decision**: Let implementation and security review loop together automatically, phase after
  phase, and save the owner's own review for one single, complete checkpoint at the end rather than
  interrupting every step.
- **Design consequence**: Became the working pattern DZP still uses today for any large,
  multi-part feature — build and verify continuously, present one finished thing for review, not a
  series of half-finished ones.
- **Benefit to others**: Large features arrive as one coherent, already-reviewed unit, not a trail
  of partially-checked pieces.

### 9. A recall feature should never be allowed to block your work if it's unhealthy

- **Date**: 2026-06-17
- **Release**: v9.5.0
- **Context**: The memory engine's recall step runs automatically before certain sensitive edits.
  The question was: if that step fails or the engine is down, should the edit be blocked?
- **Decision**: No — the recall step is advisory. A degraded or unavailable memory engine must
  never prevent you from making a legitimate edit.
- **Design consequence**: Established a permanent layering rule: the memory engine advises, but
  never gates. The actual integrity guarantee for the protocol's own historical records comes from
  a separate, always-on mechanical safeguard that has nothing to do with whether the recall feature
  happens to be running.
- **Benefit to others**: A hiccup in an optional convenience feature can never lock you out of doing
  your own legitimate work.

### 10. Make the protocol's own history queryable, not just archived

- **Date**: 2026-06-17
- **Release**: v9.5.0
- **Context**: As the project's own historical records grew and got periodically rotated into
  cold storage, that history risked becoming invisible to search — recoverable only by a person
  manually digging through old files.
- **Decision**: Bring the project's own rotated history into the memory engine's search scope,
  with an appropriately cautious trust level, rather than leave it as write-only cold storage.
- **Design consequence**: Made "what happened with this before" a question the tool can answer
  directly, while keeping older content flagged as less trusted than a document actively being
  maintained today.
- **Benefit to others**: You can ask your own project's memory tool about its own history and get
  an answer grounded in your actual past work, instead of hunting through old files by hand.

### 11. Commission the next major memory-engine upgrade the moment the previous one closes

- **Date**: 2026-06-17
- **Release**: v9.6.0
- **Context**: The first major stage of the memory engine's interconnected-recall work had just
  shipped end-to-end, with a second, larger stage already planned.
- **Decision**: Begin that second stage immediately rather than pause.
- **Design consequence**: Added structured, entity-and-relationship-aware recall combined with
  keyword-and-similarity hybrid search to the memory engine — turning it from a simple
  similarity lookup into a genuinely structured recall system.
- **Benefit to others**: You get citation-backed, structured recall rather than plain
  nearest-neighbor text matches, without ever having to ask for it — it shipped because the plan
  was carried through rather than paused after its first stage.

### 12. Declare a stable release gate, then hold to it

- **Date**: 2026-06-18
- **Release**: v9.7.1
- **Context**: The project needed a consistent, external check before anything reached the public.
- **Decision**: Declare that release gate for the memory-engine work and use it going forward.
- **Design consequence**: Fixed independent automated review as a mandatory step for every public
  release from that point on — never just the project's own internal check.
- **Benefit to others**: Every public release since has passed a review from outside the project
  itself, in addition to its own internal testing loop.

### 13. Turn an accidental footgun into a proper, opt-in feature

- **Date**: 2026-06-18
- **Release**: designed for a later release
- **Context**: A leftover machine-level setting had silently forced every local DZP install onto a
  single shared memory store, with no indication anywhere that this was happening.
- **Decision**: Don't just patch this as a bug — treat the underlying idea (deliberately sharing one
  memory across many projects on the same machine) as a legitimate feature worth designing properly,
  with the explicit requirement that it must always be visible and opt-in, never silent.
- **Design consequence**: Turned an incident into a specification: any future "share memory across
  all my projects" mode has to announce itself clearly and require an explicit choice, precisely
  because the accidental version did neither.
- **Benefit to others**: If DZP ever ships true cross-project shared memory, it will be something
  you turn on and can always see is on — not something that happens to you by accident.

### 14. Test a real upgrade against real, accumulated data before shipping it

- **Date**: 2026-06-18
- **Release**: v9.7.1 → v9.7.2
- **Context**: Every prior upgrade to the memory engine's storage format had only ever been tested
  against small synthetic examples, never a large, real, accumulated store.
- **Decision**: Before publishing, actually upgrade the team's own real, months-old memory store
  through the full chain of format changes, as a genuine test — not a simulation.
- **Design consequence**: This real-world test caught two release-blocking defects that every
  synthetic test had missed — including one that had been silently losing data in every public
  release for months. Both were found specifically because someone insisted on testing against the
  real thing.
- **Benefit to others**: Whatever size your own accumulated memory store is, the upgrade path has
  been proven against something just as large and real, not only against small test fixtures.

### 15. Fix it, ship it as its own release, and say so publicly

- **Date**: 2026-06-18
- **Release**: v9.7.2
- **Context**: The two defects found in the previous decision were fixed, but the question remained
  of how to release the fix and how to talk about the months during which the bug had existed.
- **Decision**: Cut a new, clearly-labeled release for the fix, and state plainly, in the public
  changelog, exactly which earlier releases had been affected and for how long.
- **Design consequence**: Set the standard that DZP discloses its own past defects in public release
  notes rather than quietly folding a fix into an unrelated release and saying nothing about the
  exposure window.
- **Benefit to others**: If a defect in an earlier version could have affected you, you get a plain,
  dated, public account of it — not silence.

### 16. Fully separate the day-to-day working repository from the public release repository

- **Date**: 2026-06-24
- **Release**: maintainer infrastructure
- **Context**: A routine check found that in-progress working branches were already visible on the
  same public repository meant to carry only finished releases — a real, live exposure risk.
- **Decision**: Split the project into two completely separate repositories: one private, for all
  day-to-day work and history, and one public, carrying only finished, reviewed releases — with the
  release process itself as the *only* bridge between them, and every existing branch migrated to
  the private side.
- **Design consequence**: Made it structurally impossible for in-progress work, internal history, or
  anything not meant for release to reach the public repository by any path other than the one,
  audited release process.
- **Benefit to others**: What you see in the public repository is always the deliberate output of a
  single, reviewed release step — never a leak of work still in progress.

### 17. Give the version-numbering scheme more room to grow before its next major jump

- **Date**: 2026-06-24
- **Release**: maintainer versioning policy
- **Context**: With releases coming frequently, the conventional 0–9 range for minor and patch
  version numbers would have forced an awkward jump to the next major version well before the
  protocol was actually ready for one.
- **Decision**: Widen the minor and patch version ranges from 0–9 to 0–19, giving the project
  roughly twice the runway before its next major version boundary — paired with a full check that
  every piece of tooling correctly compares version numbers numerically rather than as plain text.
- **Design consequence**: Closed a real, easy-to-miss bug class in the process (a naive text
  comparison can wrongly conclude that version "9.10" is "less than" version "9.9") before it could
  ever cause a real update-check failure.
- **Benefit to others**: Your update checker correctly recognizes a newer release as newer, with no
  version-number surprises, and the project has more releases' worth of room before it needs a
  bigger, potentially breaking version jump.

### 18. Keep sensitive data un-encrypted only where you've explicitly agreed to it

- **Date**: 2026-07-05
- **Release**: v9.9.1
- **Context**: After adding at-rest encryption for the memory engine, one legacy export path (a
  human-readable snapshot used for outside audits) still needed a plaintext option.
- **Decision**: Keep that plaintext export available, but only behind an explicit, deliberate
  choice each time — never as a silent default once encryption is enabled.
- **Design consequence**: Closed the gap between "encryption is on" and "but this one export path
  still writes plaintext by default," without breaking the legitimate audit workflow that needs a
  human-readable snapshot.
- **Benefit to others**: Turning on encryption for your own memory store doesn't leave a quiet,
  forgotten plaintext side door — any plaintext export requires you to actively ask for it.

### 19. Pay down every known small issue in one pass, rather than let it quietly accumulate

- **Date**: 2026-07-07
- **Release**: v9.9.3
- **Context**: Several minor, previously "accepted for later" issues and a documentation gap had
  been carried forward across more than one release cycle.
- **Decision**: Close every one of them now, in a single pass, rather than let the backlog keep
  growing release after release.
- **Design consequence**: Reinforced the same "bundle and finish" discipline used earlier in the
  project's history, and produced a durable, narrowly-scoped fix for one item that needed a
  targeted carve-out rather than a blanket exception.
- **Benefit to others**: You don't inherit a slowly-growing tail of "known, deferred, someday"
  issues that never actually get revisited — the project chose, at least once, to pay that debt
  down completely rather than let it compound.

### 20. Finish a release properly, and keep an unrelated research effort from entangling with it

- **Date**: 2026-07-09
- **Release**: v9.9.3 / a separate research branch
- **Context**: Two unrelated pieces of work — the routine release-maintenance line and an
  exploratory research effort — were sharing the same branch space, risking delays to one because
  of the other.
- **Decision**: Finish and publish the maintenance release through its full external-review process,
  and move the unrelated research work onto its own, fully independent branch line.
- **Design consequence**: This is also where the project's now-standard release-promotion pattern —
  point the public repository at the new, finished release and retire the review request without
  merging it, so every past release stays a frozen, inspectable artifact forever — became settled,
  repeatable practice. And an unrelated exploratory effort no longer risks delaying, or being
  delayed by, the protocol's own release cadence.
- **Benefit to others**: The release history you see stays clean and linear, each past release
  frozen exactly as it shipped; and routine maintenance releases are never held up by unrelated
  exploratory work happening in parallel.

### 21. Give the external auditor a permanent paper trail, not just a one-off report

- **Date**: 2026-07-09
- **Release**: v9.9.4
- **Context**: The project's independent, external auditor had previously produced reports that left
  no lasting trace inside the project's own historical record.
- **Decision**: Give the external auditor standing read access to the project's history, plus a
  narrow, tightly-controlled way to leave a permanent, tamper-evident note of each audit inside the
  project's own record — with full reports kept in their own dedicated, permanent location.
- **Design consequence**: Created a durable, permanent home for every external audit report, and a
  guarantee that each one leaves a lasting trace that can't be quietly discarded later.
- **Benefit to others**: Every independent audit this project has undergone since is permanently and
  verifiably part of its own history — not a report that could vanish without anyone noticing.

### 22. When two independent teams both catch the same bug, fix it once, properly, and make sure it can't happen again

- **Date**: 2026-07-09
- **Release**: v9.9.4
- **Context**: When the same protocol was set up in more than one place independently, a
  divergence appeared between two copies of the historical record for one shared work session — a
  direct side effect of having just split the project into separate lines of work.
- **Decision**: Rather than force the two copies back together immediately (which would have
  undone the separation just put in place), leave the divergence documented and separately
  reconciled later — and build a permanent, automated check to catch this specific kind of
  divergence before it ever slips through unnoticed again.
- **Design consequence**: Added a lasting, automated safeguard specifically for this failure mode,
  rather than a one-time manual fix.
- **Benefit to others**: If you ever run DZP across more than one independent line of work, there is
  now an automated check watching for exactly this kind of historical-record mismatch.

### 23. When an independent report catches something real, verify it, fix it properly, and close the loop for good

- **Date**: 2026-07-11
- **Release**: v9.9.5
- **Context**: A separate team running DZP independently found and fixed a real gap in how the
  project's secret-detection logic worked, and reported it back.
- **Decision**: Port the fix into the main project, and — while doing so — actively look for
  anything the original report might have missed, rather than simply accept the fix as-is.
- **Design consequence**: That extra scrutiny caught an additional, related gap the original report
  hadn't found, closed before anyone outside the project ever saw it — and produced a permanent,
  automated check ensuring the two related pieces of detection logic can never quietly drift apart
  from each other again.
- **Benefit to others**: The secret-detection logic protecting your own project has now been
  independently validated by more than one real-world install converging on the same fix, with a
  standing safeguard keeping it that way.

### 24. When a new safeguard could lock out brand-new installs, hold the release until it can't

- **Date**: 2026-07-18
- **Release**: v9.10.0
- **Context**: An external audit found that a brand-new safety feature — designed to enforce
  consistent identifiers on important records — would, as configured, block a fresh installation's
  very first legitimate action, with no way for a new user to work around it.
- **Decision**: Hold the entire release until that specific gap was fixed and independently
  re-verified — no partial release, no "we'll patch it after."
- **Design consequence**: Established a reusable pattern for shipping any new safeguard that could
  otherwise trap a brand-new install: ship it switched off by default for fresh installations until
  it has something meaningful to check against.
- **Benefit to others**: If you install DZP fresh today, a safety feature you haven't yet configured
  will never be the reason your very first commit gets blocked.

### 25. Bring a long-standing internal tool out of "developer-only" and into what everyone actually gets

- **Date**: 2026-07-19
- **Release**: v9.10.1
- **Context**: A central automation engine — coordinating things like session handoffs and periodic
  maintenance — had existed for a while but had deliberately never shipped to the public, out of
  caution.
- **Decision**: Ship it to everyone, now that the safety checks around it were judged solid, and
  bundle it together with a full backlog of smaller fixes that had been waiting.
- **Design consequence**: Every later feature that depends on this automation layer — session
  handoffs, the release-verification tooling, scheduled maintenance — was built on top of exactly
  the same engine every consumer now receives, not a stripped-down substitute.
- **Benefit to others**: You get the same underlying automation the project's own maintainers had
  already been relying on for several releases, not a reduced version.

### 26. When a review tool reads its rules from the wrong place, work around it rather than skip the review

- **Date**: 2026-07-20
- **Release**: v9.10.1
- **Context**: The external review tool used to gate public releases was configured to read its own
  filtering rules from the wrong side of a comparison, causing it to silently give up reviewing
  large releases entirely — twice.
- **Decision**: Build a small, dedicated helper specifically so the review tool reads the correct
  rules, rather than accept the reduced review or bypass it.
- **Design consequence**: Became a standing part of the release process going forward — every
  release since has received a genuinely substantive independent review rather than one that quietly
  gives up past a certain size.
- **Benefit to others**: Every release you receive has actually passed a real external review, not
  one that silently skipped itself.

### 27. Let an audit tool cite its own findings without special-casing away the strictness everywhere else

- **Date**: 2026-07-20
- **Release**: v9.10.2
- **Context**: A safeguard requiring every important identifier to be properly formatted and
  registered was, correctly, blocking the external auditor's own reports — because those reports
  necessarily need to cite the very identifiers they had just assigned.
- **Decision**: Add a narrow, switchable exception specifically for an audit report citing its own,
  just-assigned findings, while keeping the requirement exactly as strict everywhere else — built as
  one shared piece of logic rather than two copies that could quietly drift apart.
- **Design consequence**: Closed a recurring false alarm for exactly one legitimate case, without
  weakening the underlying safeguard anywhere else it applies.
- **Benefit to others**: Independent audit reports about your project can be committed without
  fighting the very safeguard they're documenting, while that safeguard stays just as strict for
  everything else.

### 28. Every release, verify the download against the source it actually came from

- **Date**: standing policy, first delivered 2026-07-20
- **Release**: v9.10.2
- **Context**: There was no way for someone downloading a release archive to confirm it was
  genuinely, byte-for-byte, what the project actually published — installing meant trusting the
  download blindly.
- **Decision**: Ship, with every approved release, both the release package and a signed manifest
  that lets a separate, independent tool verify the package against the project's own public source
  history before anyone installs it.
- **Design consequence**: Built a verification chain that checks the package's integrity, checks
  its own verifier hasn't been tampered with, and cross-checks against the real, public source
  repository — closing a real supply-chain gap that an early version of this very check turned out
  to have, caught and fixed during its own security review before it ever shipped.
- **Benefit to others**: You can cryptographically verify that a release you downloaded really did
  come from the project's real source history, before you ever install it — not just trust the
  download.

### 29. Don't let a documentation file quietly become a duplicated history book

- **Date**: 2026-07-20
- **Release**: v9.10.2
- **Context**: The project's own primary reference file had grown to re-tell the story of every past
  release in full, making up roughly half the file's size and duplicating content already recorded
  elsewhere.
- **Decision**: Bound that file to carry only a short summary of the current release, plus a small,
  fixed-size window of recent history — with the full, permanent history living in one dedicated
  place instead of being copied in three.
- **Design consequence**: Made this a permanent rule going forward, not a one-time trim, specifically
  so the same duplication doesn't quietly regrow with every future release.
- **Benefit to others**: The project's core reference documentation stays a manageable size that's
  actually easy to read, while the complete history remains fully available in one place, not lost.

### 30. When strict rules and real-world timing collide, rule in favor of not inventing new identifiers mid-cycle

- **Date**: 2026-07-20
- **Release**: v9.10.2
- **Context**: A release that had shipped a genuinely new capability, by the strict letter of
  version-numbering convention, should have been labeled as a bigger release than originally
  planned — but every identifier for the work involved had already been created under the smaller
  label.
- **Decision**: Keep the smaller, already-approved label for this release, and record the reasoning
  plainly for next time, along with a standing rule: settle the release's scope and its version
  number *before* creating identifiers tied to that number.
- **Design consequence**: Avoided invalidating a batch of already-created identifiers for no real
  safety benefit, while turning the tension itself into a documented lesson for future releases.
- **Benefit to others**: You get a release with a small, stable set of identifiers to track, and the
  project has a documented rule to avoid repeating this exact tension in the future.

### 31. Adopt a broader class of tracked notes as first-class, governed records

- **Date**: 2026-07-27
- **Release**: reframed the following release's scope
- **Context**: A backlog review raised the question of whether two informal note-keeping categories
  — lessons learned, and security-framework notes — should be brought under the same strict,
  tracked-identifier discipline as every other kind of tracked issue.
- **Decision**: Yes — bring them in as fully governed record types, on equal footing with everything
  else the project tracks.
- **Design consequence**: Because adding a new governed category is, by the project's own rules, a
  bigger kind of change than a routine fix, this single decision is what reframed the scope of the
  entire release that followed it.
- **Benefit to others**: Two previously informal note types now get the same append-only, verified
  discipline as every other tracked record in the project.

### 32. Don't split one release into two just to preserve a smaller version number for part of it

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: With several substantial pieces of work queued — a security bundle, a new
  session-handoff feature, a documentation and prompt-reduction pass, and the governance expansion
  from the previous decision — the release could have been split into two separate version numbers.
- **Decision**: No split. Everything ships together as one release, organized into a clear, ordered
  sequence of stages, with an explicit fallback plan to trim scope if needed — but never to fracture
  it into two closely-spaced releases with an artificial boundary between them.
- **Design consequence**: Reused the same reasoning behind an earlier versioning decision — a
  system whose update-checker compares versions for exact equality cannot tolerate a version number
  that gets skipped or never actually published.
- **Benefit to others**: You get one coherent upgrade to install and verify, rather than two
  overlapping releases in rapid succession.

### 33. Run an outward-facing security and reputation audit, and close what it finds with a permanent safeguard, not a one-time cleanup

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: With the project's public visibility growing, two urgent questions were raised at
  once: whether any internal, client-identifying references had leaked into the shipped project, and
  whether the whole project could stand up to a full outside-facing security and reputation review.
- **Decision**: Run the full audit, and treat any leaked internal references not as a one-time
  cleanup, but as a defect in the release process itself that needed a permanent, automated
  safeguard.
- **Design consequence**: Added a permanent, automatic check at release time scanning for this exact
  class of leak — proven, during its own testing, by catching dozens of real historical instances
  that had gone unnoticed until then.
- **Benefit to others**: You no longer encounter internal, project-specific references in the
  software you receive, and that protection is now a permanent part of every future release, not a
  one-off fix.

### 34. When a security feature can't be done honestly, remove it and say so — don't ship it half-working

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: The tooling needed to cryptographically sign releases turned out to be broken in the
  development environment being used, making a genuine implementation impossible to deliver
  honestly in this release.
- **Decision**: Remove the incomplete signing scaffolding entirely rather than ship something that
  looked like a real security control without functioning as one, and state the gap plainly in the
  project's public security documentation.
- **Design consequence**: Avoided creating exactly the kind of false confidence this project has
  otherwise worked hard to root out elsewhere — a control that exists in appearance but not in
  function.
- **Benefit to others**: The project's public security documentation tells you honestly that
  releases are not currently cryptographically signed, rather than implying a protection that isn't
  actually there.

### 35. One release, several major pieces of work, explicitly no phantom next release

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: With a security bundle, a new handoff feature, a documentation and framing pass, and
  a governance expansion all queued, there was a real option to spread the work across two
  version numbers.
- **Decision**: One release only. Organize the work into a clear, ordered sequence, with an explicit
  option to trim scope if needed — but never invent an extra version number that would sit unused.
- **Design consequence**: Directly reused the reasoning from an earlier versioning decision: a
  system that checks for updates by comparing version numbers exactly cannot tolerate a phantom
  version that gets renamed or skipped partway through.
- **Benefit to others**: A cleaner, more predictable release history, with version numbers that
  always correspond to something that was actually published.

### 36. Keep a nearly-empty legacy file rather than delete it, once it turns out other things depend on it

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: A cleanup pass proposed deleting an old, largely-duplicated reference file, on the
  belief that nothing depended on it anymore.
- **Decision**: Verify that belief before acting on it — and once verification found real,
  functioning dependencies on the file (in the release-safety tooling, in the project's own
  integrity checks, and in its automated safeguards), keep the file as a short, current pointer
  instead of removing it outright.
- **Design consequence**: Preserved every dependency on the file while still recovering nearly all of
  the space the cleanup had intended to reclaim.
- **Benefit to others**: Anything in the project that references this file keeps working correctly,
  while the project still gets most of the simplification it was after.

### 37. Assign ownership of two newly-governed record types to the specialists whose domain they actually match

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: Bringing lessons-learned notes and security-framework notes under strict, tracked
  governance meant deciding who within the project's structure would be trusted to create new,
  properly-formatted identifiers for each.
- **Decision**: Approved as proposed — lessons-learned identifiers are owned by the coordination
  role (since observing and recording lessons is that role's own function), and
  security-framework identifiers are owned by the security-review role (since that is squarely
  its domain).
- **Design consequence**: Assigned each governed record type to the specialist whose actual job it
  matches, using credentials both already held, rather than creating a new, centralized minting
  process.
- **Benefit to others**: Lessons-learned and security-framework identifiers are created by
  whichever part of the process actually owns that kind of judgment, not through one generic,
  centralized process disconnected from the work.

### 38. When cutting excess language, keep the parts that are true and cut only the parts that overstate what the software actually does

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: The project's distinctive character and voice made the protocol memorable and easy to
  invoke, but some of the language describing "consequences" for a misbehaving process described
  outcomes no actual mechanism enforced.
- **Decision**: Keep the character and voice — it costs little and is part of what makes the project
  what it is — but cut specifically the passages that describe enforcement no real code delivers.
  Real enforcement is a small set of automated checks and the host tool's own permission system;
  everything else is convention.
- **Design consequence**: Directly produced the plain, honest statement — now part of the project's
  public documentation — of exactly what is mechanically enforced versus what is simply agreed
  convention.
- **Benefit to others**: You get an accurate picture of what actually stops a misbehaving process
  (real, automated checks) rather than narrative describing consequences nothing in the software
  actually delivers — while the project keeps the distinctive identity that makes it memorable.

### 39. Keep a debated design choice, because narrowing it would create a worse problem than the one it solves

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: A design choice in the project's identifier-tracking system — deliberately keeping a
  broad, permissive matching rule to catch accidental duplicate identifiers — was flagged as
  possibly too broad.
- **Decision**: Keep it as-is. The same session that raised the question, the broad rule had already
  caught a real duplicate identifier that a narrower rule would have missed — and narrowing it would
  make a large number of older, genuinely ambiguous historical references permanently unresolvable,
  training a habit of routinely overriding the safeguard instead.
- **Design consequence**: A deliberate, reasoned "keep it as-is" decision, on the record, rather than
  a silent non-fix — with the actual trade-off spelled out for future maintainers.
- **Benefit to others**: The identifier-tracking system stays effective at catching real accidental
  duplicates, without forcing routine use of an override flag to work around old, ambiguous history.

### 40. Retire a claimed capability that had no real code behind it, rather than resurrect it just to keep the claim

- **Date**: 2026-07-28
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: A previously-documented safety feature turned out to have no actual code path
  reaching it anywhere in the project — the same category of "documented but not wired" gap the
  project had already found and fixed elsewhere in this same release.
- **Decision**: Formally retire the claim rather than rebuild the feature just to make the
  documentation true — consistent with the same standard applied to every other instance of this
  problem found this release.
- **Design consequence**: Applied a hard-won lesson consistently, even to a low-stakes case, rather
  than making an exception because the stakes were small.
- **Benefit to others**: The project's documentation doesn't claim a safety capability that has no
  code actually backing it — and if that capability is ever genuinely rebuilt, it will be done
  properly, with a real, tested code path, not resurrected only to restore an old claim.

### 41. Make sure the new "hand off your session" feature is offered exactly when someone is tired enough to need it

- **Date**: 2026-07-29
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: While building a new feature for safely handing off a session's context to a fresh
  one, a gap was noticed: the project's existing fatigue-monitoring alerts (which fire after long
  work sessions) didn't yet mention this new option at all.
- **Decision**: Add the new hand-off feature to every fatigue alert, at every severity level,
  alongside the existing save/pause/end options.
- **Design consequence**: Every fatigue alert now offers a way to safely stop working without losing
  the thread of what you were doing, not just a choice between saving and stopping cold.
- **Benefit to others**: When you get a fatigue warning, you now have a genuinely useful way to step
  away without losing your place.

### 42. Require a dedicated, adversarial review before cutting language from the project's own agent files

- **Date**: 2026-07-29
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: Before trimming the character-voice language discussed above, the project's own
  process required a dedicated, deliberately skeptical review of the plan first.
- **Decision**: Require that adversarial review to formally clear the work before any of it could be
  implemented — not as a formality, but as a real, binding gate.
- **Design consequence**: The review's conditions genuinely reshaped the final implementation —
  including requiring that the final change be described using a real, measured result rather than
  an earlier, more optimistic estimate.
- **Benefit to others**: The specific language cuts that shipped to you are the version that
  survived a dedicated, skeptical review looking specifically for overreach — not the first draft of
  the idea.

### 43. Build this very report — a public account of the project's own decision history

- **Date**: 2026-07-29
- **Release**: v9.11.0
- **Context**: No mechanism existed for turning the project's own internal decision history into a
  readable, public account of why it's built the way it is — the gap this document is the answer
  to.
- **Decision**: Build exactly that — one internal, full-detail draft reviewed by the project owner
  first, and a separate, paraphrased public edition that must pass an automated safety check before
  it can ship, with generation restricted to one specific role and no new access granted to anyone
  to produce it.
- **Design consequence**: Produced a two-stage process where the public account of the project's own
  decisions is itself gated by a mechanical check, not a promise — the same principle the whole
  project applies everywhere else, applied here to its own origin story.
- **Benefit to others**: You are reading the result of that decision right now.

---

## What this record cannot tell you, and why that's stated plainly

This report is honest about its own limits, on principle. Domain Zero Protocol's earliest history —
the origin of its multi-agent structure, its tiered workflow system, its safety-first operating
principles, its emergency-stop mechanism, and the very append-only record-keeping rule this report
relies on — is real, shipped, and documented in the project's public release notes in detail. What
it is *not* is independently, dated, and attributably recorded as a specific decision in the way
every entry above is, because the internal record capable of carrying that attribution simply did
not exist yet in that form during that period.

Rather than paper over that gap with invented detail, this report says so directly. As the
project's own decision-recording practice matures, future editions of this report should have
progressively fuller, more precisely-dated coverage of more recent history. That the earliest era
is thinner is disclosed here rather than smoothed over — because a project that hides its own
coverage gaps would be doing the opposite of what this whole report is trying to demonstrate.

---

**This document is regenerated, not hand-edited, each time it is refreshed** — and it is refreshed
only with the project owner's explicit approval, tied to a specific release.
